questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Total Displacement of a Particle Given Its Velocity
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t$ is given by $v(t)=2t-\sqrt{t}.$ What is the total displacement of the particle between $t=0$ and $t=9?$
questions.worked_solution:
We find the total displacement by calculating the definite integral of the velocity.

Let $d$ be the total displacement. Then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={\int }_{0}^{9}(2t-\sqrt{t})\text{d}t \\  & ={({t}^{2}-\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2})|}_{0}^{9} \\  & =[(9)^{2}-\frac{2}{3}(9)^{3/2}]-[(0)^{2}-\frac{2}{3}(0)^{3/2}] \\  & =81-18-0 \\  & =63.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the total displacement between $t=0$ and $t=9$ is $63.$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t$ is given by $v(t)=12{t}^{2}-4t.$ What is the total displacement of the particle between $t=0$ and $t=3?$
questions.worked_solution:
We find the total displacement by calculating the definite integral of the velocity.

Let $d$ be the total displacement. Then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(12{t}^{2}-4t)\,\text{dt} \\  & ={(4{t}^{3}-2{t}^{2})|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =[4(3)^{3}-2(3)^{2}]-[4(0)^{3}-2(0)^{2}] \\  & =[108-18]-0 \\  & =90.\end{aligned}
$$

So the total displacement between $t=0$ and $t=3$ is $90.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Final Position of a Particle
questions.problem:
A particle $Q$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t\ge 0$ is given by $v(t)={2}^{2t-1}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2).$ At time $t=1$ the particle is located at the position $x=-5.$ 
Find the position of the particle at time $t=3.$ Do not round the answer.

The position of the particle at $t=3$ is $x=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=3$ is equal to its position at $t=1$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [1,3].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(3)=x(1)+{\int }_{1}^{3}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(3) & =-5+{\int }_{1}^{3}({2}^{2t-1}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2))\,\text{d}t \\  & =-5+{[{2}^{2t-2}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =-5+{2}^{2(3)-2}-{2}^{2(1)-2} \\  & =-5+{2}^{4}-{2}^{0} \\  & =-5+16-1 \\  & =-5+15 \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the position of the particle at $t=3$ is $x=10.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Final Position of a Particle
questions.problem:
A particle $Q$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t\ge 0$ is given by $v(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).$ At time $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ the particle is located at the position $x=5.$ 
Find the position of the particle at time $t=\pi .$ Do not round the answer.

The position of the particle at $t=\pi $ is $x=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=\pi $ is equal to its position at $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [\frac{\pi }{2},\pi ].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(\pi )=x(\frac{\pi }{2})+{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(\pi ) & =5+{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =5+{[\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)]}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =5+[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )]-[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =5+(0-1)-(1+0) \\  & =5-2 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the position of the particle at $t=\pi $ is $x=3.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Final Position of a Particle
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t>0$ is given by $v(t)=2t+{t}^{2}.$ At time $t=1$ the particle is located at the position $x=4.$ What is the position of the particle at time $t=3?$
questions.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=3$ is equal to its position at $t=1$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [1,3].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(3)=x(1)+{\int }_{1}^{3}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(3) & =4+{\int }_{1}^{3}(2t+{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =4+{[{t}^{2}+\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =4+([{3}^{2}+\frac{{3}^{3}}{3}]-[{1}^{2}+\frac{{1}^{3}}{3}]) \\  & =4+([9+9]-[1+\frac{1}{3}]) \\  & =4+(18-\frac{4}{3}) \\  & =4+\frac{50}{3} \\  & =\frac{62}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the position of the particle at $t=3$ is $x=\frac{62}{3}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Final Position of a Particle
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t>0$ is given by $v(t)={e}^{2-t}.$ At time $t=1$ the particle is located at the position $x=e.$ What is the position of the particle at time $t=2?$
questions.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=2$ is equal to its position at $t=1$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [1,2].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(2)=x(1)+{\int }_{1}^{2}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(2) & =e+{\int }_{1}^{2}{e}^{2-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =e+{[-{e}^{2-t}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =e+([-{e}^{2-2}]-[-{e}^{2-1}]) \\  & =e+([-{e}^{0}]-[-{e}^{1}]) \\  & =e+(-1+e) \\  & =2e-1\end{aligned}
$$

So the position of the particle at $t=2$ is $x=2e-1.$

questions.problem:
A particle $Q$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t\ge 0$ is given by $v(t)={e}^{t}+3.$ At time $t=0$ the particle is located at the position $x=-{e}^{2}.$ 
Find the position of the particle at time $t=2.$ Do not round the answer.

The position of the particle at $t=2$ is $x=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=2$ is equal to its position at $t=0$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [0,2].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(2)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{2}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(2) & =-{e}^{2}+{\int }_{0}^{2}({e}^{t}+3)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{e}^{2}+{[{e}^{t}+3t]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =-{e}^{2}+({e}^{2}+3(2))-({e}^{0}+3(0)) \\  & =-{e}^{2}+({e}^{2}+6)-(1+0) \\  & =-{e}^{2}+({e}^{2}+5) \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the position of the particle at $t=2$ is $x=5.$

$$

$$
{\int }_{1}^{6}v(t)\,\text{d}t=\frac{3}{2}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
x(6)=2+\frac{3}{2}=\frac{7}{2}.

So the position of the particle at $t=6$ is $x=\frac{7}{2}.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Total Displacement of a Particle Given Its Velocity
canonical_examples.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t$ is given by $v(t) = 2t + 3t^2.$ What is the total displacement of the particle between $t=1$ and $t=3?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We find the total displacement by calculating the definite integral of the velocity.

Let $d$ be the total displacement. Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(2t+3{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={({t}^{2}+{t}^{3})|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =[{3}^{2}+{3}^{3}]-[{1}^{2}+{1}^{3}] \\  & =[9+27]-[1+1] \\  & =36-2 \\  & =34.\end{aligned}
$$

So the total displacement between $t=1$ and $t=3$ is $34.$

canonical_examples.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t>0$ is given by $v(t) = 6t^2 +4t.$ At time $t=2$ the particle is located at the position $x=-20.$ What is the position of the particle at time $t=4?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=4$ is equal to its position at $t=2$ plus the total displacement over $t\in[2,4].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(4) = x(2) + \int_2^4 v(t)\,\textrm{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(4) & =-20+{\int }_{2}^{4}(6{t}^{2}+4t)\,\text{dt} \\  & =-20+{[2{t}^{3}+2{t}^{2}]}_{2}^{4} \\  & =-20+([2(4)^{3}+2(4)^{2}]-[2(2)^{3}+2(2)^{2}]) \\  & =-20+([128+32]-[16+8]) \\  & =-20+(160-24) \\  & =-20+136 \\  & =116.\end{aligned}
$$

So the position of the particle at $t=4$ is $x=116.$
